title: The Road No Ship Finds: Pindar, Pytho, and the Seventeen Books
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Thebes, the sixty-fifth Olympiad
stops.date_confidence: Traditional. The Alexandrian chronographers assign the birth to the 65th Olympiad, conventionally c. 518 BCE; no contemporary document fixes the year, and the ancient Lives are centuries later than the man. Month and day are defaults. Coordinates inherit the atlas pin for Thebes.
stops.campa: The chronographers put his birth in the sixty-fifth Olympiad, which the moderns count as about 518, and the city they name is Thebes, in Boeotia, a country the rest of Greece calls slow. No document fixes the year and no house is pointed out. The Lives that supply the details are written centuries after the man they describe, and they are all anyone has. What stays put is the ground: the citadel they call the Cadmea, a plain of grain and horses, a dialect Athenians mock, a shrine at every crossroads.
suggested_refs: The Cadmea, the acropolis of Thebes in Boeotia
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pindar', summarizing the ancient chronographic tradition
P.Oxy. XXVI 2438, the papyrus Life of Pindar

stops.name: Cynoscephalae, the village of the Dog's Heads
stops.date_confidence: Traditional and unlocated. Some ancient Lives give Cynoscephalae rather than Thebes itself; the site has never been fixed on the ground and these coordinates are an approximate placement near Thebes, not a located village. The two birthplace traditions are not reconciled here.
stops.campa: Other Lives put the birth not in the city but at Cynoscephalae, a village outside it whose name means Dog's Heads, after a pair of hills standing up like a hound's ears above the road. The two accounts are not reconciled by anything; they sit side by side in the ancient tradition, and the village has never been located. The name has drawn confusion of its own, since travellers' books elsewhere in Greek writing describe a race of men with dogs' faces at the edge of the world. These are hills.
suggested_refs: The Boeotian toponym Cynoscephalae, 'Dog's Heads', a name given to paired hills
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pindar', on the variant birthplace tradition
Research note on the Cynoscephalae / Cynocephali confusion; the specific ancient citation (Vita Ambrosiana or the Suda) was not retrievable in this pass

stops.name: Thebes, the bees at the mouth
stops.date_confidence: Legend, undated. The bee story is a standard inspired-infant topos in ancient biography, attached to other poets and philosophers as well; the date is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: The story the ancients tell about the infant is that bees settled on his lips while he slept and left honey there, and that this is why the verse comes out sweet. The same bees have been reported at other cradles, over other sleeping poets and philosophers, in the same kind of book. It is a sign attached to a career after the career is finished, read backward into the crib. Pindar does use a bee himself, once, in Pythian 10, and it is not an infant's: the praise-song, he says there, 'flitteth like a honey-bee from tale to tale.'
suggested_refs: The bee-on-the-lips topos in ancient Lives of poets and philosophers
sources: Ancient Lives of Pindar, per Wikipedia, 'Pindar'
Pindar, Pythian 10, the honey-bee image at lines c.51-54

stops.name: Thebes, the fathers the Lives cannot agree on
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The ancient Lives disagree; nothing here can be dated. The stop is placed in boyhood to order the segment.
stops.campa: Ask the ancient biographers who his father was and three names come back: Daiphantus, Pagondas, Scopelinus. They do not argue with one another; each Life states its own name and moves on. The mother is more stable, usually Cleodice. Nothing settles the disagreement, and the disagreement is itself the evidence: a biographical tradition assembled late, out of scraps, rather than kept from the start. Which name a Theban of the fifth century would have given, no source is in a position to say.
suggested_refs: The variant paternities in the ancient Lives: Daiphantus, Pagondas, Scopelinus
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pindar', collating the ancient Vitae

stops.name: Thebes, the matter the poems are made of
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, from the content of the surviving odes rather than from any biographical record. The date orders the segment and marks nothing.
stops.campa: The stock of the trade is there before he touches it: the Ionian epics of Homer, the hexameter Hesiod set down for a Boeotian farm and for a genealogy of the gods, the local cult-lists, the Delphic religion, the family trees of aristocratic houses that need their ancestors sung. A choral poet does not invent that matter. He selects from it and cuts it to fit one man who has won a footrace, and the cutting is where the labour goes. Most of the genealogies come out of Hesiod's Catalogue of Women.
suggested_refs: Hesiod's Theogony and Catalogue of Women as sources of the genealogical material worked into the epinikia
sources: Standard account of Pindar's poetic formation, per Wikipedia, 'Pindar' and the surviving odes themselves

stops.name: Athens, the school of Lasus of Hermione
stops.date_confidence: Late tradition only. The apprenticeship under Lasus, and the rival tradition naming Agathocles, come from the ancient Lives; no contemporary word confirms either, and no date is transmitted. Placed c. 505 for order.
stops.campa: Late sources send the young Theban to Athens to study with Lasus of Hermione, a poet and theorist of music who had worked at the court of Hipparchus and is credited with bringing the dithyramb into competition there. Others in the tradition name a second teacher, Agathocles. No contemporary word confirms either name, and no date is transmitted for the journey. What the odes show, independently of the Lives, is technical schooling of some kind: strophe answering antistrophe in exact metre, triads built to be sung and danced at once by a chorus that has to be drilled into them.
suggested_refs: Lasus of Hermione, music theorist at the Peisistratid court
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pindar', summarizing the ancient Vitae

stops.name: Tanagra, sow with the hand and not the whole sack
stops.date_confidence: Anecdotal tradition, undated, and contested at the root: modern scholars dispute Corinna's own dates, and some place her long after Pindar, which would make the whole exchange impossible. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: In Boeotia there is another poet working, Corinna of Tanagra, and the tradition makes her his teacher, his critic, and his rival by turns. She looks at a poem of his stuffed with myth and tells him to sow with the hand and not the whole sack. She is said to have beaten him five times in competition; he is said to have answered by calling her a Boeotian sow. Modern scholars dispute her dates, and some put her a century and more after him, which would leave nobody in the room for any of it.
suggested_refs: Corinna of Tanagra, and the modern dispute over her dating
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pindar', citing the ancient anecdotal tradition

stops.name: Mount Helicon, a god heard singing a mortal's paean
stops.date_confidence: Legend, undated. The story that Pan was heard singing a paean of Pindar's is normally cited to Pausanias 9.23; Book 9 could not be retrieved from any open text this session, so the citation is secondhand. Coordinates inherit the atlas pin for Mount Helicon.
stops.campa: In the hill country west of Thebes, the commentators say, Pan was heard singing one of Pindar's paeans, the god performing the mortal's words. Pindar composes a hymn to Pan in return, or perhaps before; the order is not recorded. Pausanias is the authority usually given for the story. It is the same mountain where Hesiod says the Muses came down to him while he was pasturing lambs, breathed a voice into him, and put a staff of cut laurel in his hand.
suggested_refs: Pindar's hymn to Pan, surviving in fragments
The Valley of the Muses below Helicon
sources: Ancient Lives and commentary tradition, per the research dossier; normally cited to Pausanias 9.23, unverified this session

segments.name: Pytho, 498: The Road No Ship Finds

stops.name: Delphi, the boys' double stadion
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the ancient scholia, which date Pythian 10 to 498 BCE; this is the earliest securely dated surviving poem. Month and day are defaults. Coordinates inherit the atlas pin for Delphi.
stops.campa: At the Pythian games in the sanctuary of Apollo a boy from Thessaly, Hippocleas of Pelinna, wins the diaulos, twice the length of the stadium, out and back. The scholia date the ode written for him to the year the moderns count as 498. Its author is about twenty. Everything earlier that he wrote is gone, so the surviving work begins here, not with a hymn to a god but with a commission from a Thessalian dynasty for a boy's footrace. The poem is Pythian 10, the earliest Greek victory ode that carries a secure date.
suggested_refs: The stadium and the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi, site of the Pythian games
sources: Pindar, Pythian 10, with the scholia vetera supplying the 498 BCE date
W. H. Race, Pindar, Loeb Classical Library (1997), vol. I

stops.name: Pelinna, the father who ran twice in armour
stops.date_confidence: Attested as text: Pythian 10.4-5 names Pytho, Pelinna, and the Aleuadae, and the ode credits Phricias with two Olympic victories in the race in armour. Pindar's own presence at Pelinna is not attested. Coordinates corrected to the ancient town site at Palaiogardiki.
stops.campa: The victor's town sits in the Thessalian plain, and his father Phricias is a name already known at Olympia, where he won twice in the race run in armour, helmet and shield carried the length of the track. The ode names Pytho, Pelinna, and the Aleuadae in one breath, as the three forces that call the song out. A boy's win is never only a boy's win in this poetry; it is one more entry in a family record, and the family pays for the entry. Phricias's two crowns are named in the ode before his son's one.
suggested_refs: Pelinna (Pelinnaion) in Thessaly, at the site of Palaiogardiki near Trikala
The hoplitodromos, the Olympic race run in armour
sources: Pindar, Pythian 10.1-16 (Race, Loeb, 1997)
Wikipedia, 'Pelinna', for the location of the ancient town

stops.name: Larissa, the Aleuadae buy a song
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Thorax of the Aleuadae is named in the ode as its commissioner. The political reading is modern (Pavlou, Mnemosyne 76: 375-393, DOI 10.1163/1568525x-bja10107); the article's full text was not retrievable, so its argument is reported at second hand.
stops.campa: Thorax, head of the Aleuad house that rules from Larissa, commissions the ode. His family holds Thessaly the way the Heraclid kings hold Sparta, and the poem opens by saying exactly that, blessing Lakedaimon and Thessaly together as two countries under one bloodline. A modern reading takes the whole ode as local politics, addressed past the victor to the Thessalian nobles and to the Amphictyonic council that runs Delphi. Hippocleas is named in the first triad. The Aleuadae are in it from the first line to the last.
stops.quote: Happy is Lakedaimon, blessed is Thessaly: in both there reigneth a race sprung from one sire, from Herakles bravest in the fight.
stops.quote_source: Pindar, Pythian 10, opening lines, trans. Ernest Myers, The Extant Odes of Pindar (Macmillan, 1874)
suggested_refs: The Aleuadae of Larissa, ruling house of Thessaly
Maria Pavlou, 'Localizing Pindar's Pythian 10', Mnemosyne 76 (2023): 375-393
sources: Pindar, Pythian 10 (Race, Loeb, 1997; Myers translation via Wikisource)
Crossref record for DOI 10.1163/1568525x-bja10107

stops.name: Delphi, the road no ship finds
stops.date_confidence: Attested as text, Pythian 10.27-30. The stop is pinned at Delphi because that is where the ode was sung; Hyperborea is declared unreachable by the poem itself and is given no pin.
stops.campa: The ode reaches the limit of what a man may have and states it: nobody climbs the bronze heaven, but every splendour open to mortals this boy has now touched. Then it turns north, toward the people who live beyond the north wind, and shuts the door in the same breath that opens it. There is no way there. Not by sea, not on foot. The poem is sung in Apollo's own sanctuary, and the country it declares unreachable is the country where Apollo is said to be happiest.
stops.quote: But neither by taking ship, neither by any travel on foot, to the Hyperborean folk shalt thou find the wondrous way.
stops.quote_source: Pindar, Pythian 10, lines c.29-30, trans. Ernest Myers, The Extant Odes of Pindar (Macmillan, 1874)
suggested_refs: Pindar, Pythian 10.27-30, the gnomic statement of mortal limit before the Hyperborean excursus
sources: Pindar, Pythian 10 (Myers translation via Wikisource; Greek text Snell-Maehler)
Christopher G. Brown, 'The Hyperboreans and Nemesis in Pindar's Tenth Pythian', Phoenix 46 (1992): 95-107

stops.name: Delphi, Perseus at the feast of asses
stops.date_confidence: Attested as text, Pythian 10.31-36. A mythic scene sung at Delphi, not a place anyone travelled to; the pin records where the ode was performed.
stops.campa: One man got there, and he was not a traveller: Perseus, leader of his people, walked into the Hyperborean halls and ate with them. He found them killing donkeys for Apollo, whole hecatombs of them, and the god delighting in the racket and laughing at the beasts' braying insolence. Greek prestige sacrifice runs on cattle. Here it is the wrong animal entirely, going under the knife by the hundred at the far edge of the world, and Apollo is laughing.
stops.quote: Yet of old the chieftain Perseus entered into their houses and feasted among them, when that he had lighted on them as they were sacrificing ample hecatombs of asses to their god.
stops.quote_source: Pindar, Pythian 10, lines c.31-33, trans. Ernest Myers, The Extant Odes of Pindar (Macmillan, 1874)
suggested_refs: The donkey hecatomb of the Hyperboreans, an inversion of ordinary Greek prestige sacrifice
sources: Pindar, Pythian 10 (Myers translation via Wikisource)
Brown, Phoenix 46 (1992): 95-107

stops.name: Delphi, the people without sickness or age
stops.date_confidence: Attested as text, Pythian 10.37-44. Pinned at the performance site; the Hyperboreans are given no coordinates because the poem denies that any road reaches them.
stops.campa: The Muse never leaves them. Girls dance in rings, lyres sound with the shrill pipes cutting across them, golden bay is bound in every head of hair, and the feasting does not stop. No plague comes to that country and no wasting old age; they do not work and they do not fight, and Nemesis, who levels every mortal that rises too far, has no jurisdiction there. It is the exact inventory of everything the victorious boy standing in the sanctuary is going to lose.
stops.quote: Nor pestilence nor wasting eld approach that hallowed race: they toil not neither do they fight, and dwell unharmed of cruel Nemesis.
stops.quote_source: Pindar, Pythian 10, lines c.41-44, trans. Ernest Myers, The Extant Odes of Pindar (Macmillan, 1874)
suggested_refs: Nemesis, the retribution that falls on mortals who rise too high, absent among the Hyperboreans
sources: Pindar, Pythian 10 (Myers translation via Wikisource)
Brown, Phoenix 46 (1992): 95-107

stops.name: Delphi, the anchor out of the prow
stops.date_confidence: Attested as text, Pythian 10.44-54. Same pin and same reason as the preceding stops in this segment.
stops.campa: Athena leads Perseus on from the feast to the Gorgon's head and the stone death of the men of Seriphos, and there the poet stops himself in the middle of the myth. He calls for the oar to be let go and an anchor driven into the ground from the prow, before the ship strikes the reef. The praise, he says, goes from story to story like a honey-bee, and a bee does not steer. Then the ode turns back, in that order, to the boy from Pelinna and to the men who paid for it.
stops.quote: Let go the oar, and quickly drive into the earth an anchor from the prow, to save us from the rocky reef, for the glory of my song of praise flitteth like a honey-bee from tale to tale.
stops.quote_source: Pindar, Pythian 10, lines c.51-54, trans. Ernest Myers, The Extant Odes of Pindar (Macmillan, 1874)
suggested_refs: The metapoetic anchor, Pindar's device for breaking off a mythic excursus
sources: Pindar, Pythian 10 (Myers translation via Wikisource)

stops.name: Larissa, a friend for a friend
stops.date_confidence: Attested as text for the praise of Thorax and of unnamed brothers. The brothers' names, Eurypylus and Thrasydaeus, are supplied by the ancient scholia and are not in the poem; the two are kept apart here and not merged.
stops.campa: The close of the ode names the patron plainly and thanks him for the labour of getting it made: Thorax yoked this four-horse chariot of the Muses, a friend doing it for a friend. Then it praises his brothers for holding up the traditional laws of the Thessalians. The poem does not give those brothers names. Eurypylus and Thrasydaeus come from the scholia, centuries later, and are quoted as Pindar's own by readers who never go back to the line. Whether the scholiasts knew or guessed cannot now be established.
stops.quote: My trust is in the kindly courtesy of my host Thorax, of him who to speed my fortune hath yoked this four-horse car of the Pierides... His noble brethren also will we praise, for that they exalt and make great the Thessalians' commonwealth.
stops.quote_source: Pindar, Pythian 10, closing lines, trans. Ernest Myers, The Extant Odes of Pindar (Macmillan, 1874)
suggested_refs: The scholia vetera on Pythian 10, source of the names Eurypylus and Thrasydaeus
sources: Pindar, Pythian 10 (Myers via Wikisource; Perseus/Svarlien text checked for the absence of the names)

segments.name: Medism, and the Bulwark of Hellas

stops.name: Thebes, the city that medized
stops.date_confidence: The Theban medism is attested (Herodotus 9.31-32 puts Theban troops in the Persian line at Plataea). Pindar's personal conduct is not documented by any contemporary text; Polybius 4.31, three centuries later, is a hostile reading of a Pindaric fragment, not a record of what the poet did.
stops.campa: Xerxes comes down through Thessaly and Boeotia, and the faction ruling Thebes goes over to him; Theban troops stand in the Persian line at Plataea and fight there against the rest of Greece. What Pindar does in those two years is nowhere recorded by anyone writing at the time. Three centuries later Polybius quotes a Pindaric verse counselling the citizens to seek the light of lordly Peace, and names the poet as the man who talked Thebes into the inaction that earned it disgrace.
suggested_refs: Polybius, Histories 4.31, on Pindar and Theban quietism
sources: Polybius, Histories 4.31 (penelope.uchicago.edu)
Herodotus 9.31-32 for the Theban contingent at Plataea
Wikipedia, 'Pindar'

stops.name: Athens, bulwark of Hellas
stops.date_confidence: The fragment (fr. 76) is well attested in the later quotation tradition; its performance venue, occasion, and date are not. The story of an Athenian reward and a Theban fine is anecdote with no judicial or civic record behind it.
stops.campa: A fragment survives in which Athens is hailed as the bulwark of Hellas, and it comes from the poet of a city that had just fought on the other side. The anecdote grown around it has Athens paying him and Thebes fining him for the same handful of words, with the Athenian gift covering the Theban penalty twice over. Later writers quote the line constantly, and it is on their quotation that its survival depends. No decree, no court record and no dated document supports the fine, the payment, or the occasion the words were sung for.
suggested_refs: Pindar fr. 76, the dithyrambic praise of Athens, quoted by later authors
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pindar', on fr. 76 and the fine anecdote

stops.name: Athens, the statue in the marketplace
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Pausanias 1.8.4, who saw the statue and reports the Athenian explanation of it; he gives no erection date, so this date is an ordering device only and the monument may well be posthumous.
stops.campa: Pausanias, walking through Athens six centuries later, passes a bronze of Pindar and writes down what the Athenians told him about it: they gave him the statue because he praised them in an ode. It stands near an image of the lawgiver Calades, among the honours the city hands out to men who are not its citizens. When it went up nobody says. A Theban, in bronze, in Athens, for a compliment paid during a war the two cities fought on opposite sides of.
stops.quote: obtained this statue from the Athenians because he praised them in an Ode
stops.quote_source: Pausanias, Description of Greece 1.8.4, trans. Frazer/Jones, Project Gutenberg ebook 68946
suggested_refs: The honorific statues near the Athenian agora described in Pausanias 1.8
sources: Pausanias, Description of Greece 1.8.4, fetched directly (Project Gutenberg 68946)

stops.name: Syracuse, Ortygia and the horse of Hieron
stops.date_confidence: The commission and the 476 BCE date are attested by the ode itself and the standard epinician chronology. Pindar's personal presence in Sicily is an inference from the commissions, not a documented journey; the court-rivalry stories with Simonides and Bacchylides are late scholiastic inference.
stops.campa: Hieron rules Syracuse and half of Greek Sicily, and in 476 his horse wins at Olympia. From here the Theban is inside the richest patronage market in the Greek world, working for tyrants who can pay for anything and who need, more than they need another racehorse, a poem that makes their power look like something a god arranged. The ode written for the horse opens the collected Olympians, and it opens by ranking the elements: water is best, and gold shines out at night above lordly wealth like a blazing fire.
suggested_refs: Olympian 1, the opening ode of the Alexandrian collection
sources: Pindar, Olympian 1 (Race, Loeb, 1997)
Wikipedia, 'Pindar', dated victory-ode chronology

stops.name: Acragas, the ridge of temples
stops.date_confidence: The commissions for Theron and Thrasybulus are attested by the odes themselves (Olympian 2, Olympian 3 and related poems, 476-470s). Travel to Acragas is inferred from the commissions and asserted only by late Lives.
stops.campa: West along the Sicilian coast, Theron rules Acragas from a ridge lined with temples, and he and his kinsman Thrasybulus take their turn as patrons. The odes written for that house handle wealth and rule at arm's length, setting out what a rich man owes, what the dead are judged for, and what the gods do to men who forget which of the two they are. Whether Pindar ever stood on the ridge is not attested anywhere. The commissions are certain; the journey is an inference drawn from them.
suggested_refs: Olympian 2 and Olympian 3, for Theron of Acragas
The Valley of the Temples at Acragas
sources: Pindar, Olympian 2 and 3 (Race, Loeb, 1997)

stops.name: Olympia, where the wins are made
stops.date_confidence: General across the career rather than a single event; the date orders the segment. Fourteen Olympian odes survive, composed across several decades, and the individual victories are dated by the ancient victor lists and scholia.
stops.campa: The victories the odes celebrate are won here, in the precinct of Zeus, across five days of festival every four years. The poems are not performed here. They are sung at home, once the victor is back with the wild olive on his head and the town has turned out for him. Pindar works this ground for four decades, for a Sicilian tyrant's stable and for a boy from a small town on the same terms. Fourteen of the forty-five complete odes that survive are Olympian.
suggested_refs: The Temple of Zeus and the stadium at Olympia
The fourteen surviving Olympian odes
sources: Pindar, Olympian Odes (Race, Loeb, 1997)
Wikipedia, 'Pindar'

stops.name: Aetna, the city under the mountain
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Pythian 1 is dated to 470 BCE and takes Hieron's chariot victory and the foundation of Aetna as its occasion. The coordinates are those of Catania, on the site Hieron refounded.
stops.campa: Hieron clears the people out of Catania and refounds the place as Aetna, under the mountain, with his own son Deinomenes installed to rule it. In 470 his chariot wins at Delphi and he has himself proclaimed as Hieron of Aetna, not of Syracuse. The ode written for that victory takes the new city as its business. It opens on the lyre whose sound puts even the eagle of Zeus to sleep, then sets the monster Typhos pinned and burning under the mountain, then turns and talks to the founder at length, quite directly, about ruling by law rather than by fear.
suggested_refs: Pythian 1, for Hieron of Aetna, 470 BCE
The refoundation of Catania as Aetna under Deinomenes
sources: Pindar, Pythian 1 (Race, Loeb, 1997)
Wikipedia, 'Pindar'

segments.name: The Four Sanctuaries and the Long Middle Years

stops.name: Nemea, the book that is not all Nemean
stops.date_confidence: The eleven Nemean odes are a fact of the transmitted corpus; the individual dates vary and several are disputed. The date here orders the segment. Coordinates are those of the sanctuary of Zeus at ancient Nemea.
stops.campa: Eleven odes come down under the name of this sanctuary in the Argolid, where the games are held for Zeus and the crown is wild celery. Not all eleven were won here. The Alexandrian editors, arranging the corpus centuries afterward, used the Nemean book as the place to put odes that fitted none of the other three, so the heading names a festival and also names a filing decision. Which of the eleven were won at Nemea is argued ode by ode and settled for none of them.
suggested_refs: The sanctuary of Zeus at Nemea
The eleven Nemean odes and the Alexandrian arrangement
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pindar'
Race, Pindar, Loeb (1997), introduction on the Alexandrian books

stops.name: Isthmia, the book that breaks off
stops.date_confidence: The eight complete Isthmian odes are a fact of the transmitted corpus; the date orders the segment. The medieval manuscripts stop after Isthmian 8 and Race prints a fragmentary Isthmian 9, so the loss is at the end of the book, not the beginning. Coordinates are those of the sanctuary of Poseidon at Isthmia.
stops.campa: The fourth festival stands on the neck of land at Corinth, in the sanctuary of Poseidon, and Pindar writes for its victors as he writes for the other three. Eight of those odes survive whole. The medieval manuscripts break off after the eighth, and a ninth exists only as a fragment, so the Isthmian book is damaged at its end rather than its opening. Forty-five complete victory odes reach the modern world in all. Everything else the man wrote is quotation and papyrus.
suggested_refs: The sanctuary of Poseidon at Isthmia
The fragmentary Isthmian 9 printed after the eight complete odes
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pindar' for the counts 14/12/11/8
Race, Pindar, Loeb (1997), for the fragmentary Isthmian 9

stops.name: Aegina, the island of the Aeacids
stops.date_confidence: The proportion of Aeginetan odes is a straightforward count from the surviving corpus and is attested; the dates run from the 490s to the 450s and the stop is placed mid-range. Residence on the island is not established by the count and is not claimed here.
stops.campa: A quarter of the surviving victory odes are for men of this one small island, more than for Athens, Thebes, and Sparta together. The Aeginetan families paying for them want the same ancestors sung each time: Aeacus, Telamon, Peleus, Ajax, Achilles, the hero line the local cult is built on. The temple of Aphaia looks across the strait toward Attica from the ridge above. Whether the poet lived there in stretches, or only sent the poems and the rehearsal instructions across, no source says.
suggested_refs: The Temple of Aphaia on Aegina
Anne Pippin Burnett, Pindar's Songs for Young Athletes of Aigina (2005)
sources: Count of Aeginetan victors in the surviving corpus, per Wikipedia, 'Pindar'

stops.name: Lindos, the ode in letters of gold
stops.date_confidence: The ode and its 464 BCE occasion are attested. The gold inscription in the temple of Athena Lindia is unverified tradition: no stone survives and no ancient inventory lists it.
stops.campa: Diagoras of Rhodes, a boxer of enormous fame, wins at Olympia in 464, and the ode made for him tells how the island came up out of the sea for Helios and how the Rhodians once forgot the fire for their sacrifice and were rewarded anyway. Tradition says the poem was cut in letters of gold and set up in the temple of Athena on the acropolis at Lindos, on the rock above the harbour, where anyone coming ashore would have had to look up at it. No stone has been found. No ancient inventory lists it.
suggested_refs: The Temple of Athena Lindia on the acropolis of Lindos
Olympian 7, for Diagoras of Rhodes
sources: Pindar, Olympian 7 (Race, Loeb, 1997)
Wikipedia, 'Pindar', for the gold-inscription tradition, flagged there as unverified

stops.name: Cyrene, the longest ode and a man in exile
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Pythian 4 and 5 honour Arcesilas IV and are dated 462/461 BCE. Whether Pindar knew Damophilus personally, or performed any assigned diplomatic role, is unresolved.
stops.campa: For Arcesilas, king of Cyrene on the Libyan shore, Pindar writes the longest victory ode there is: the whole Argonaut voyage, Medea's prophecy, the clod of earth that turns into the island of Thera, and the descent of the royal house from a settler out of Sparta. Then, at the end, in front of the assembled court, the poem turns to the king and asks him in plain words to let an exile named Damophilus come home. A commission bought for a chariot win is doing diplomatic work in public. Whether the poet knew the exile is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: Pythian 4, the longest surviving victory ode, and its plea for Damophilus
The sanctuary of Apollo at Cyrene
sources: Pindar, Pythian 4 and 5 (Race, Loeb, 1997)
Wikipedia, 'Pindar', dating the pair to 462/461 BCE

stops.name: Delphi, a dream of a shadow
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Pythian 8, for Aristomenes of Aegina, is tied to the Pythian victory of 446 BCE and is the latest securely dated ode in the corpus. The famous closing phrase is quoted from the ode in many translations; no single verbatim rendering was verified in this pass, so none is given as a quote.
stops.campa: Aristomenes of Aegina wins the wrestling at Pytho in 446, and the ode for him is the last that can be securely dated. It describes what the boys he threw are going home to, slinking down back alleys out of sight of their enemies, and then it says what all of them are: creatures of a day, the dream of a shadow, until a brightness given by a god comes down and the life turns sweet. The poet is past seventy. Nothing later than this survives with a date attached to it.
suggested_refs: Pythian 8 and its closing formulation on human beings as the dream of a shadow
sources: Pindar, Pythian 8 (Race, Loeb, 1997)
Wikipedia, 'Pindar', for the 446 BCE date

segments.name: Persephone, Theoxenus, and the Road to Argos

stops.name: Thebes, the Mother of the Gods next door
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated. The scholia and Pausanias report both a vision and a cult founded near the poet's house; Pausanias Book 9 could not be retrieved from any open text this session, so the citation is secondhand. A real local shrine is easier to credit than the apparition.
stops.campa: Near his own house in Thebes there is a shrine of the Mother of the Gods, and the commentators say Pindar founded it, or paid for it, after a flame appeared or a stone image moved and the goddess showed herself to him. Pausanias, walking the city centuries afterward, records the monuments and the local claim. The shrine is easier to believe than the apparition. Which came first, the cult at the door or the story that explains why it is there, the record does not distinguish.
suggested_refs: The shrine of the Mother of the Gods at Thebes, reported by Pausanias near Pindar's house
sources: Scholia and Pausanias, per the research dossier; Pausanias Book 9 not retrievable this session

stops.name: Argos, the boy from Tenedos
stops.date_confidence: The fragment is attested; its date, occasion and place of composition are not. It is placed here only because the death legend attaches Theoxenus to the poet's last hour at Argos. Nothing establishes that the fragment was written there.
stops.campa: A fragment survives, numbered 123, addressed to a young man called Theoxenus of Tenedos, and it states desire without cover and without apology. It is the plainest erotic writing left in the corpus, and it sits inside the ordinary conventions of aristocratic Greek lyric rather than outside them. The legend fastens Theoxenus to the poet's last hour, which may be nothing more than the tradition joining the two most quotable things it holds. Where and when the lines were written, nobody knows.
suggested_refs: Pindar fr. 123, addressed to Theoxenus of Tenedos
sources: Standard citation of Pindar fr. 123 in classical scholarship; not re-fetched from a critical edition in this pass

stops.name: Argos, the death at eighty
stops.date_confidence: Traditional. Death at Argos at about eighty, conventionally c. 438 BCE, comes from the late Lives; no contemporary notice survives and the variant accounts of the manner of death are not reconciled. The only firm bracket is Pythian 8 of 446 BCE.
stops.campa: He dies at Argos, about eighty years old, and the ancient Lives cannot agree how. One says in the theatre. One says resting on the shoulder of Theoxenus. One says Persephone came to him beforehand, complaining that she was the only deity he had never hymned, and that ten days after his death he appeared to a kinswoman in a dream and dictated the poem he owed her. No contemporary notice of the death exists. The record simply stops after the ode of 446 and does not resume.
suggested_refs: The competing death legends in the ancient Lives: the theatre, Theoxenus, and Persephone's complaint
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pindar', collating the ancient Vitae
Research dossier's collation of the variant death legends

stops.name: Thebes, the daughters bring the ashes home
stops.date_confidence: Late tradition. The names Eumetis and Protomache, the carrying of the ashes, and the Theban burial are all from the late Lives; nothing contemporary confirms any of it, and the date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Late sources name two daughters, Eumetis and Protomache, and say they carried their father's ashes back from Argos to Thebes for burial. Nothing contemporary confirms the names, the journey, or the grave. The city that takes him back is the one whose medism the rest of Greece never let go of, and whose laws and heroes he had spent sixty years setting to music for other people's sons. Out to Delphi, Sicily, Aegina, Cyrene, for a working lifetime; home in a jar.
suggested_refs: The traditional grave of Pindar at Thebes
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pindar', and the late biographical tradition

segments.name: The Chair, the Books, the House

stops.name: Delphi, the iron chair and the supper of the gods
stops.date_confidence: Posthumous honour of unknown original date. The only witness is Pausanias 10.24.5, writing in the second century CE; the passage could not be fetched from Perseus, Theoi, Wikisource, Attalus or Gutenberg this session and is reported at second hand. The date is an ordering device with no evidential value.
stops.campa: At Delphi they kept an iron chair and said it was the one Pindar sat in when he came to the god's house, and at the Theoxenia, the feast where the gods are hosted as guests, a herald called out his name and invited him to the supper. He had been dead for centuries by the time Pausanias saw the chair and wrote the custom down. Once a year, a poet who is not there is called to the table of the god he wrote paeans for. When the honour began, and who started it, nobody records.
suggested_refs: The iron chair of Pindar at Delphi and the Theoxenia summons, reported at Pausanias 10.24.5
sources: Pausanias 10.24.5, via Wikipedia, 'Pindar'; primary text not reachable this session

stops.name: Thebes, the house left standing
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the bare fact: Arrian, Anabasis 1.9, says Alexander preserved the house and the descendants of Pindar out of respect for his memory. The motive usually attached, that Pindar had praised an ancestor of the Macedonian kings, is not in Arrian and belongs to a later strand of the tradition. Coordinates and date inherit the atlas pin for the Theban stop on alexander.journey.json.
stops.campa: Thebes revolts against Macedon, is stormed, and is taken apart stone by stone; the people are killed or sold. Alexander gives an order that one house is to be spared, and the house is Pindar's, together with his descendants, for the sake of a poet who had lived in it a hundred and thirty years before. Arrian records the sparing and stops there. The reason usually attached to it, that Pindar had written verses praising an ancestor of the Macedonian kings, comes from later writers and is not in Arrian at all.
stops.quote: It is said that Alexander preserved the house and the descendants of Pindar the poet, out of respect for his memory.
stops.quote_source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 1.9, English Wikisource text
suggested_refs: The house of Pindar at Thebes, the sole dwelling left standing in 335 BCE
Plutarch, Life of Alexander 11, for the parallel account
sources: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 1.9 (en.wikisource.org, fetched)

stops.name: Alexandria, seventeen books by kind
stops.date_confidence: Attested as transmission history: the seventeen-book arrangement by genre belongs to Hellenistic Alexandrian scholarship, associated with the tradition of Aristophanes of Byzantium, and is illuminated by P.Oxy. 2438. The date is a placement inside the Hellenistic period, not an event date. Pindar himself never went to Alexandria; the stop is for the corpus.
stops.campa: In the library the scholars sort him out: seventeen books arranged by kind, hymns, paeans, dithyrambs, processionals, maiden-songs, dance-songs, encomia, laments, and four books of victory odes, an arrangement associated with Aristophanes of Byzantium. He is set among the nine lyric poets who are to be copied and taught. Of the seventeen books, the four victory-ode books come through whole and the other thirteen break into quotations and scraps of papyrus. Forty-five poems out of seventeen books.
suggested_refs: The Alexandrian canon of nine lyric poets
The seventeen books of Pindar in the Alexandrian edition
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pindar'; Race, Pindar, Loeb (1997), introduction

stops.name: Oxyrhynchus, a Life in the rubbish mound
stops.date_confidence: The papyrus is dated on palaeographic grounds to the late second or early third century CE; the date given here is that palaeographic bracket, not a documented year. Published as P.Oxy. XXVI 2438 in 1961. Pindar never went to Egypt; the stop is for the document.
stops.campa: In the rubbish mounds of a provincial Egyptian town, buried among tax receipts and shopping lists, lies a damaged papyrus copy of a Life of Pindar, written out around the turn of the third century after Christ by somebody who wanted the facts about a poet seven hundred years dead. Published in 1961 as P.Oxy. 2438, it is a first-rank witness to how the Alexandrian edition was ordered. The biography it carries is the same late and uncertain tradition, attested five centuries earlier than the medieval Lives. Somebody threw it out with the kitchen rubbish.
suggested_refs: P.Oxy. XXVI 2438, the papyrus Life of Pindar
E. L. Bundy, Studia Pindarica (1962), which reoriented reading of the odes from biography to the rhetoric of praise
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pindar', on P.Oxy. 2438
